newsitem.title: UK: Pearson exec sees opportunity in Internet.
newsitem.headline: Pearson exec sees opportunity in Internet.

text.p: Media owners and marketers need to adapt to the changing marketplace afforded by the Internet, with a greater focus on customising products, Marjorie Scardino, chief executive of Pearson Plc, said on Monday.

Scardino, speaking before the Advertising Association's annual meeting, said she was not a "media prophet of doom" and said the Internet is only a tool rather than a technology that will change the world.
She painted a picture of a world where the Internet will allow a greater customisation of products, but where traditional mass marketers will continue to play a major role.

"Had I been in this spot a couple years ago, I might have come as a media prophet of doom," Scardino said. At that time, she said, she might have predicted that the Internet would fragment media markets and make existing mass marketing obsolete.
But while the Internet offers opportunities rather than posing a threat, Scardino said the media need to act to remain on top of changes in technology.
"Newspapers used to be in the vanguard of technology," said the chief executive of Pearson, whose interests include the Financial Times and the Economist.
"Now most of us have out-of-date systems ... and have let others get ahead of us," she said.
Being able to connect personal computers to the Internet is revolutionary, she said. "The Internet animates and integrates all our markets and all of us.
"But computers and the Internet, as it turns out, are not a new art," Scardino added. "They do not produce life. They're not mysterious. They're pipes, very powerful pipes."
The new technology allows the delivery of timely, in-depth information on a personalised basis, meaning that the media and marketers must adapt to the new environment.
"A lot of the ways we think are going to have to change," she said, noting the need to target individuals rather than always aiming at mass markets.
But Internet technology remains limiting in many ways, including frequent problems logging on to the global computer network and unwieldy methods of searching for relevant web sites.
There are also questions about the ability to earn reasonable returns on Internet investments.
"All of this suggests to me that mass marketing still has a place," Scardino said.
